confused with stratification and covariates. I can send a copy of my data=

ad Sodota) in Bale Mountains National Park, Ethiopia.I visit the same=20

finding out if there are regional variations in the different types of=20=

livestock densities AND if there is temporal variation in livestock=20
densities within a region (wet/dry season).

One of the issues I have been having is that the number of sightings=20
differ between species (fewer horse sightings)but also between regions=20=

(fewer sightings in Sanetti).I read in the DS book than I could have=20
stratify by data by species, use a global detection function and get=20
encounter rates per stratum. Since I can only use one level of=20
stratification, it means that I need to have three different datasets (on=
e=20
for each region)and analyse them separately. Which means that I have to=20=

analyse Sanetti on its own and there are fewer sightings there so likely=20=

bigger CI in the end.

Also, it would make sense to use the fact that I go back to the same=20
transects every time to increase my sample size of sightings to give me a=
=20
better detection function for each area. In which case, do I use data as =
a=20
covariate alongside stratifying for species? Does that mean that distance=
=20
computes a global (?)detection function across dates but you can obtain=20=

encounter rates per sampling session?Is this what the MCDS do?How do I go=
=20
on about it?

I'd like now to understand how I will ultimately have to analyse the data=
=20
to analyse trends through time and between regions...any help would be=20=

greatly appreciated.

wondering if anyone has been successful in obtaining funding (and where)i=
n=20
the past ...

Flavie Vial

messages.author: 5140016d70f6ba82
messages.subject: Re: stratification by species and time as covariate?
parts:
Flavie-

First of all, I laud your thinking to know how your data will be
analyzed prior to its collection.

The original intent of strata was spatial and/or temporal strata. Using
species or some other observation covariate
was not its original intent. The CDS/MCDS engines are a bit inadequate
in coping with multi-levels of stratification.
Also, I can empathize with your confusion. It is important to
differentiate in your mind between covariates and strata and how they
should be used. The problem here is that there is overlap between the
two. First and foremost, strata are used to define
the subset of the data for density calculations. They define
geographic, temporal or observation subsets. For example, I want
horse density in region 1 during the wet season. On the other hand,
covariates in DISTANCE are ANY variables that can influence
the detection probability of objects. Therein lies the confusion,
because variables used to define the strata can also be covariates
that affect detection probability. So covariates can include strata
variables. Let's say you thought that detection probability might be
different for each species for each region in each season. One obvious
simple solution is to define a strata for each species-region-season
combination and estimate its detection function and density. Then the
total abundance of horses in the season can be computed by
adding the abundances across the 3 regions. But it is very unlikely
that you can get a sufficient number of sightings of each species in each
region and season to estimate an adequate detection function. Thus,
you want to estimate a global model for detection that can share
the data across the strata while compensating for potential differences
in detection probability. This is where you think about how strata
variables can be used as covariates in the detection probability. In
the first case that I outlined, the covariate model for the detection
function
could be viewed as a full interaction model (region*season*species) in
which there is a different scale parameter (eg sigma in a half-normal) for
each combination of region,season and species. While all of these
variables may influence detection probability, it may not be necessary
to propose
such a complex model and one might think of an additive model in which
region+species+season is adequate or maybe you believe that certain
interactions are necessary. Based on the biology and your knowledge of
the sampling, you need to decide what are a set of plausible models to
explore. You can then fit a candidate set of models and use model
selection to ascertain the most parsimonious model from your candidate set.

Now, that was actually the easy part. Given that you derive an adequate
detection model, if it is not region*season*species, then when you go to
put together the estimates of abundance, the point estimates are fairly
easy but the variance estimates get messy due to the covariances that
now exist
because you used a common detection function. In the case of
region*season*species, it would be equivalent to having independent
detection functions
so there would be no covariances (but that is not likely to happen).
For the time being, let's ignore season and think of species and
region. If all I want to do
is estimate abundance of each species for each region and get a total
abundance for each species for all regions, then the analysis is rather
straightforward.
I believe Buckland et al 2001 contain the formula for handling the
covariances in this case. Len or someone else will have to tell you if
and how this can be done
with the MCDS engine. I can tell you that with the MRDS engine (using
single observer survey) it is relatively straightforward. You would
define strata based on
region and provide their areas. In one analysis, you would use all of
your data (all species,regions,seasons) to fit the best detection
function. Then in separate
analyses for each species, you would use the data filter to select the
species and for detection function you choose the analysis containing
your final detection function
model. MRDS will provide the density and abundance for each region and
for all regions combined and it will account for the covariances in
detection across
strata (region in this case). You can repeat that for each species.
Not what it will NOT do is provide the covariances in density/abundance
between species estimates. If all you want is total livestock abundance,
for each region, you can avoid that problem by not filtering by species
and getting a total abundance for all livestock within
each region and for all regions. This avoids tying to construct a
variance estimate for total livestock abundance from the separate
species estimates and variances because
you won't have the covariances to include. Now if you want those
covariances, then you should get them from MRDS if you use
region-species as your strata and give
the same area size for each species within a region. You can get each
density/abundance for each region-species and it will give you the v-c
matrix, but then you'll have to do the calculation for total abundances.

Now, let's consider season. If you want to get an abundance for each
species in each season. Then filter by season and species and you can
get a density/abundance for each region and the total across regions.
But now you have the same problem when you want to compare species
abundance between seasons. Like as above, if you use season-region as
the strata, then MRDS will give you the v-c matrix and you can do the
calculations by hand.

As you can see MRDS is not going to solve all of your problems. What is
missing in the software is a way to specify a formula for abundance and
a method of specifying the sampling structure. All assume a fairly
simple structure of lines sampled within a set of regions. MRDS gives
you the potential to account for covariances but is not as flexible as
it needs to be. However, if you know R you can use the mrds package
separately and then you can provide your own flexibility for these
calculations.

There is a lot of development going on currently to provide spatial
modelling capabilities for abundance which will provide the capability
to specify a formula for the abundance model (ie abundance covariates)
as well as detection function covariates. This moves distance sampling
into a spatial context as it should be. That still leaves an open
question of how to handle time (season) but the obvious next step is to
move to space-time models for abundance.

regards--jeff
